doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Themes and style of his lyrics: distilled and timeless
summary: Amy and Audre describe his lyrics as pithy, distilled and unconnected to specific events.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Amy, you’ve studied a lot of your dad’s lyrics, or you’ve just absorbed them...
I just know them.
What would you consider to be... Are there themes in common that they have? Are there certain registers or keys he likes to write for? Tell me whatever you care to analytically about...
It’s very specific, and it’s very much him. And it’s funny, and it’s ironic lots of times. No?
I used to write for a scale, B-flat at the top. But I sang sometimes up there, but I used to... “Seventh Son” is in B-flat, and...
But what about your lyrics? He was talking about your lyrics?
Well, B-flat was the top of my scale. I used to sing E-flat above that, and sometimes... But I remember writing for a scale of B-flat.
How complicated were your melodies? Did you ever put in things, for instance, that seem simple but there’s a lot of complex information underneath that you make...
No, I didn’t think about that.
Amy, let’s get back to the lyrics. You know these lyrics probably as well as anybody. What are some of the constant themes you perceive in his lyrics, just as stories?

Oh my God. I mean, it’s hard for me to think about that. Themes. Hmm. They’re very cosmic, kind of philosophical but very diluted, like really the opposite... Or it’s very economical. And very pithy. Like, he would take really...find a really...
Sort of refine from something more complex.
Distilled.
Distilled.
That’s what I meant, not...
Like Walter Pater said, “art is the removal of surplus.”
That’s what I always thought, is that he said a whole lot in a very pithy, concise,
and powerful way, and it would be a lot of really deep things...
And a lot of things that don’t refer to any specific thing happening in the world, because that’s why, over and over again, people think, “Oh, he just wrote that song.”
They have a timeless quality, don’t they.
Yes.
Like, Diana Krall could be singing two of his songs now, and they sound like...
